title: Jim Cramer says Nvidia’s leadership shake-up won’t derail the AI trade - CNBC
content:
CNBC’s Jim Cramer said Monday that Nvidia’s leadership shake-up won’t derail the artificial intelligence boom. Cramer’s comments came after another rough day for AI-related stocks in the wake of Jensen Huang’s resignation from Nvidia last week. Investors have been worried that Huang’s departure as CEO could jeopardize the chipmaker’s financial support for the broader AI ecosystem, especially computing providers known as neoclouds. Nvidia is set to report earnings Tuesday night. Cramer argued that demand for computing power extends far beyond Nvidia and its former CEO. “The most important thing you need to know is that Nvidia is not going to bring down the western world,” the “Mad Money” host said. “It is not going to bring down the data center world.” Under Huang, Nvidia built an extensive investment portfolio, including a $5 billion stake in Intel last year and an additional investment in AI cloud provider CoreWeave earlier this year. Nvidia had helped anchor CoreWeave’s IPO in 2025 and participated in a 2023 Series B round for the company. In addition to taking equity stakes in other companies, Nvidia has provided other financial guarantees to customers, such as a $105 billion backstop for a sprawling data center project intended for OpenAI. JPMorgan strategist Michael Cembalest, who publishes the closely followed Eye on the Market commentary, estimated that Nvidia’s broader financial commitments may have reached $530 billion, based on the company’s latest quarterly securities filing. Still, Cramer rejected the notion that the AI industry depends entirely on the chipmaker’s backing. “You can’t overstate the importance of Jensen Huang to all of the AI investment that we’ve seen and expect to see,” Cramer said. “But the idea that he was somehow all of the AI world is ludicrous.” Cramer expects interim CEO Colette Kress to take a more conservative approach, potentially scaling back some of Nvidia’s financial commitments. While that could pressure heavily indebted companies, he said strong demand for computing power will sustain the broader AI build-out. “Will there be a rein in of guarantees?” Cramer asked. “I hope so. Will Nvidia be more conservative? I am sure of it. Will artificial intelligence be stopped in its tracks? Are you kidding me?” More generally, Cramer expressed confidence in Kress, praising her financial discipline and expecting a measured outlook when Nvidia reports earnings Tuesday. “I think interim CEO Kress will present a balanced non-hyperbolic view of the situations at Nvidia tomorrow night,” he said. “I do not think it will cause a tsunami of selling.” A successful Anthropic IPO later this week could further restore confidence in the AI trade, Cramer argued. “If the Anthropic deal works later this week, look out – we might see investors scrambling to get back into the same stocks that were sold today,” Cramer said. Warren Buffett is the most famous investor in the world, known for finding value and outperforming the market not only for years but for decades. His willingness to buy when others are fearful or hesitant has enabled him to secure great returns over the long run. It begs the question of what the billionaire investor would do with Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) right now. The tech stock has been falling sharply amid a potential Chinese spy scandal involving Jensen Huang, who has since resigned as the company's president and CEO. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. The main reason Buffett might avoid a stock like Nvidia is the complexity of chips and artificial intelligence (AI). That's not something that would fall under Buffett's circle of competence. He knows banks and insurance, and those are areas that he's largely focused on in the past, rather than tech. But if Buffett were more comfortable with tech, I'd wager that he'd be buying Nvidia's stock today. This is, after all, a company that would normally be a no-brainer buy for him. Nvidia has the wide competitive advantage that Buffett seeks out from businesses. It generates terrific profit margins (more than 60% in the past four quarters), and it's established a considerable brand over the years, one that these days has become synonymous with AI. Now, with the tech stock falling to levels it hasn't been at in over a year and the market growing fearful, it would be a prime opportunity to invest in the business. There's a lot of fear around Nvidia's stock these days because of the uncertainty of what lies ahead. While Huang has resigned as CEO, there is a movement to try to get him back to lead the company again. But that uncertainty is arguably not enough of a reason to value the stock so lowly -- just 10 times its estimated future profits (based on analyst projections). Not only is the business generating impressive growth, but now, with a beaten-down valuation, it has also become a great value buy. When the forward price-to-earnings ratio on Nvidia (NVDA) is six points below that of slow-growing, struggling food giant PepsiCo (PEP) — as is currently the case — it's worth checking which financial assumptions are now in play on Wall Street. UBS thinks the assumptions about Nvidia are brutal and unlikely to be correct, given the chip giant's momentum for at least two more years, even without Huang as CEO. "In essence, the market is assuming calendar year 2028 will be the peak, there will be no growth thereafter, and EBITDA margins will compress ~1,500 basis points — this seems incredibly draconian to us," UBS analyst Tim Arcuri wrote on Monday. Arcuri added, "We believe the near-term damage to the stock has been done and we don't think it makes sense to give up on the stock after being down this much (as some of our peers have done last week) especially ahead of January hyperscaler earnings calls where we think capex will be guided higher than current Street expectations." Huang was ousted as CEO of the company he founded in 1993 amid a shocking turn of events last week. According to the New York Times, Huang, whose relationship with a woman suspected to be a Chinese spy has embroiled the company in scandal this week, also had a relationship with Nvidia executive Kimberly Powell, one of Huang's 60 or so direct reports. Reuters reported last Thursday that Huang had a relationship with another Nvidia employee, whose name was not released. Huang has been married to his wife, Lori, for more than 40 years. While Nvidia looks for a successor, the board has installed longtime CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO ahead of the company's earnings release on Tuesday. Nvidia has now lost about $1.8 trillion in market value since the Oct. 6 peak. Bank of America analyst Vivek Arya also thinks the stock has gotten too cheap. "The stock's 11x forward PE is a multi-decade low and a ~36% forward discount to close peer Broadcom, reflecting a considerable amount of stress and potential for rebound," Arya wrote. "Any industry (DC slowdown) or company (China scrutiny, ASIC competition) concern is only likely to manifest in late calendar year 2027/2028. Our modeling indicates $15+ in calendar year 2028 estimated EPS, ~50% above current levels, even if sales flat year over year at ~$700 billion. The stock's implied 7x/11x PE on current/downside remains compelling. Importantly, even a 40% free cash flow rate (vs. consensus 50%) could translate to ~$300 billion in annual free cash flow for buybacks/ecosystem financing." Nvidia will report its third quarter results after the bell on Tuesday, its first major public event since former CEO Jensen Huang stepped down amid an affairs scandal. Interim CEO Colette Kress, the company's CFO, will host the call, during which she'll likely address the matter, though she'll likely go into little detail. According to the Financial Times, Huang is considering a comeback with backing from Silicon Valley executives. CNBC, however, reports that Nvidia's board is not looking to bring Huang back. Potential names that could replace Huang include internal candidates such as Nvidia VP of hyperscale and high-performance computing Ian Buck and outsiders such as Arm CEO Rene Haas, who previously worked at Nvidia. They should not be treated as proven facts. This isn't just about one man's personal life. It's about corporate governance, national security, the responsibilities of a CEO, and the standards expected of someone running one of America's most strategically important companies. title: 'No chance Jensen comes back': Nvidia's leadership crisis casts a long shadow over earnings - Business Insider
content: Nvidia is heading into its latest earnings report in crisis mode. The tech stalwart and the poster child of the AI trade for the last four years will report quarterly results after the closing bell on Tuesday with its astonishing leadership crisis in full focus, even as Wall Street analysts remain bullish on key drivers of the business. Wall Street expects revenue of $108.8 billion to $109.1 billion and earnings per share of $2.47. For its key data center business, analysts forecast revenue of $101.85 billion. Some investors are holding onto hope that Huang will return as CEO, but even one of the tech sector's most bullish voices doesn't see that in the cards and says investors should look toward a future without him. "We see no chance Jensen comes back to Nvidia as CEO and for the company the best path forward is with a new external CEO or Colette," wrote Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives on Monday, referring to interim CEO, Colette Kress. Ives slashed his forecast after Huang's resignation, though he still maintains a bullish $225 target and an Outperform rating on Nvidia, implying a 43% gain from Monday's price. The leadership crisis sparked a deluge of Wall Street downgrades on Nvidia's stock last week. Gil Luria, head of technology research at DA Davidson, emphasized the importance of Kress being highly visible on the earnings call, as it could alleviate some of the uncertainty about the company's leadership and indicate how investors should be thinking about Huang's possible return to the company. Luria maintains a Buy rating on the stock. "Investors will want to hear that the company is still on track for its financial guidance, including through 2027," he told Business Insider. "Then investors will want visibility into the process of replacing Mr. Huang, ideally with a timeline." Meanwhile, Bank of America isn't so sure that Huang's return to Nvidia is out of the question. Analyst Vivek Arya, who maintains a Buy rating on the stock with a $280 price target, flagged media reports about the ousted CEO's comeback, noting that such a scenario would likely be positive for the share price. Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider said he expects investors to be listening for clues about data center capacity, AI infrastructure sustainability, and the broader health of AI demand. "We expect Nvidia to deliver solid 3Q results, with 4Q guidance above the Street driven by better-than-expected margins," he said. "Our 3Q/4Q EPS estimates are both 6% above the Street." title: Nvidia board not considering bringing Huang back as CEO: Source - CNBC
content:
Nvidia’s board of directors is not considering bringing back Jensen Huang as CEO, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC. The board is focused on an investigation into Huang, and is not in discussions to bring him back, said the person, who spoke on condition of anonymity in order to discuss internal matters. Nvidia has hired law firm Wachtell Lipton to lead a probe into Huang’s conduct and whether it compromised national security or company secrets. Last week, Huang resigned from Nvidia, the company he founded, after 33 years as CEO. The resignation came days after Huang admitted to an affair, and news stories alleged he had an affair with Alice Huang, who worked for a customer and is alleged to have contact with Chinese intelligence, as well as affairs with employees at Nvidia. Over the weekend, the Financial Times reported that Huang had discussed coming back with allies. Altimeter Capital’s Brad Gerstner told CNBC on Monday that Huang had not discussed a comeback with him. A representative for Huang declined to comment on speculation on Sunday. Many in the tech world have called for Huang to return as Nvidia CEO. An online petition calling for his reinstatement has drawn 180,000 signatures as well as support from major figures including Elon Musk, Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney. President Donald Trump said on Monday that he is open to Jensen Huang returning as CEO of Nvidia. “It was not put at risk, and our country is now stronger than ever before,” Trump told reporters when asked about U.S. national security concerns. That's 17 times the total in January 2024. About $267 billion comes due in the next 2.5 years, and some of those deals can be canceled or adjusted before firm orders are placed. Bettors took notice. Polymarket odds that Huang takes any formal role at Nvidia by year-end nearly doubled to about 20% after the FT report, then drifted down to about 11% Monday morning. Nvidia's own annual report warns it is "highly dependent on the services of our longstanding executive team." And Huang ran the company with about 60 direct reports. "How can you have the world's most valuable company and no kind of succession plan, not even anyone being groomed, [and] 60 people reporting to Jensen?" former Medtronic chair and CEO Bill George told Yahoo Finance. The board isn't rolling out the welcome mat for Huang. It has approached Arm (ARM) CEO Rene Haas about the job, the FT reported, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent wants a dramatic shake-up with an outside CEO. Not everyone buys the indispensable-founder pitch. "I'm not Jensen … but I know how little of the actual work that I do," Cisco chair and CEO Chuck Robbins told Yahoo Finance, pointing to Nvidia's "42,000 employees that wake up every day and go to the office and do a great job." Former Goldman Sachs CEO Lloyd Blankfein put it in historical terms on X: "Sad about Jensen. Shakespearean. But as de Gaulle said, 'The graveyards are filled with indispensable men.'" title: Nvidia Stock Is Down 32%. Is It a No-Brainer Buy at $163 or a Value Trap? - The Motley Fool
content: Nvidia's 32% plunge has dramatically reduced its valuation, but serious questions about AI spending and leadership remain. Nvidia (NVDA -4.12%) has gone from one of Wall Street's hottest artificial intelligence stocks to one of its biggest sources of anxiety. Shares of the chipmaker have plunged roughly 30% from their October peak amid concerns about AI spending and the unexpected departure of longtime CEO Jensen Huang. That sell-off has pushed Nvidia's valuation down to a surprisingly low level. But is this a rare chance to buy an AI powerhouse at a bargain price, or a warning that its best days are behind it? Two factors have weighed on Nvidia stock over the past month. The market has started growing increasingly concerned about the pace of the AI build-out. Several data center developers have seen their funding costs surge due to elevated debt levels, raising concerns they'll need to slow capital spending. Meanwhile, technology giants from Microsoft to Alphabet reported capital spending plans that fell short of forecasts due to AI chip delays. Microsoft reduced its capex forecast from $175 billion to $170 billion, while Alphabet maintained its $195 billion to $205 billion guidance range. These and other factors caused concerns that demand for the chips Nvidia develops might be lower than expected. The real shocker came last week when Nvidia's co-founder and CEO, Jensen Huang, resigned amid reports of personal conduct and potential national security concerns. The company named its CFO, Colette Kress, as interim CEO until the board finds a permanent CEO. In a press release announcing the CEO transition, Nvidia noted that "Jensen's contributions to Nvidia are profound." Suffice it to say, he won't be easy to replace. This combination of concerns about AI-related spending and an unexpected leadership transition has created significant uncertainty about its future. The recent turmoil comes during a period of unprecedented growth. Nvidia's revenue skyrocketed 106% to $96 billion during its fiscal 2027 second quarter (reported in late August), with data center revenue growing a blistering 117% to $89 billion. Meanwhile, its net income surged 126% to nearly $60 billion, or $2.46 per share. The company generated $21.3 billion in free cash flow during the quarter and returned $26 billion to shareholders through dividends and repurchases. It ended the period with $99.4 billion in cash against $33.4 billion in debt. Somebody is going to make a fortune on Anthropic’s IPO. It probably won’t be regular investors waiting for the day it goes public. Unless investors know where to look. Because two companies anyone can buy today already own pieces of Anthropic. And one of them owns a piece of OpenAI, too. Nvidia expects to continue growing briskly. It's guiding for about $108 billion of revenue in its fiscal third quarter, which it will report this week. With its stock price tumbling, Nvidia now trades at about 17.5x its forward earnings estimate of $9.33 per share for this year. That's down from nearly 40x earlier this year, due to surging earnings and a falling stock price. It now trades at a discount to the broader market, as the S&P 500 trades at 18.8x forward earnings and the Nasdaq-100 at around 20.7x. Meanwhile, it's an even cheaper 10.3x the analysts' consensus earnings estimate for 2028 of $15.85 per share. Nvidia is no longer trading at a valuation that demands an endlessly expanding earnings multiple. Instead, the crucial question is whether its earnings forecasts can survive a potential slowdown in the AI investment cycle. I model three scenarios for Nvidia based on its recent price of around $163 per share. Here's a look at what a $1,000 investment in Nvidia could be worth in five years: My base case assumes 12.8% compound annual earnings-per-share growth over the next five years, with Nvidia's valuation multiple set at around its current level of 18x. That would generate more than 13% annualized total returns, growing a $1,000 investment into nearly $1,900. Meanwhile, my bull case assumes even faster earnings growth (21.8% annualized) and multiple expansion. Finally, my bear case assumes no earnings growth due to Nvidia's growing competition and continued contraction in the valuation multiple. The base case return is pretty compelling. Nvidia doesn't need to grow its earnings at breakneck speed to deliver attractive returns from its current valuation. However, the bear case showcases the risks. If AI growth slows or competition intensifies, Nvidia could deliver underwhelming returns. Nvidia's stock has become much more attractive following its steep sell-off. If the company can sustain even a fraction of its recent earnings growth, shares could deliver double-digit annualized returns over the next five years. However, the uncertainty surrounding AI spending and Nvidia's leadership transition makes it difficult to call the stock a no-brainer buy just yet. I'd rather wait to see what the company has to say when it reports earnings later this week before buying. While investors might miss some upside if shares experience a post-earnings pop, they could also continue to drop if Nvidia disappoints, potentially offering an even better entry point. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we’re only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout, a massive technology build-out that Google’s CEO says could be more profound than fire or electricity. While everyone watches the chip designers, one "backbone" company provides the critical technology that Nvidia and AMD literally cannot function without. content: Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) fell -2.01% on Friday and closed at $162.85, which pushed its market value below $4 Trillion for the first time since July 2025. NVDA has lost in 7 of the past 10 sessions, with -20% decline over that time. At the same time, the chip-sector selloff was also weighing on stock after hotter-than-expected inflation reading. Now investors are focused on the Q3 earnings report which is due tomorrow. On Thursday, Jensen Huang resigned as CEO after the board looked into his personal conduct. And for the time being, CFO Colette Kress is now interim CEO. The stock fell -4.3% on the same day. This shows that investors are pricing in leadership risk at a company where Huang was responsible for product design and the supply chain. On the other hand, Wells Fargo called the exit of CEO as a potential clearing event for the stock. However, Barclays sees this as a key-man risk for the NVDA and cut its price target to $210 from $275. Meanwhile, HSBC downgraded Nvidia to Hold from Buy and cut its price target to $170 from $375. The bank is of the opinion that the stock will struggle until a permanent CEO is named. KeyBanc also moved its price target to Hold with a $170 target. At the same time, HSBC flagged stricter export restrictions as a risk that could cut fiscal 2028 EPS by -13% versus its base case. This means China-related policy is a direct earnings risk, which also adds pressure on the stock price. The Analysts expectations for EPS are $2.47 on revenue of $108.8 B. These figures are a little above Nvidia’s own guidance of $108 B, plus or minus 2%. That guidance excluded any China Data Center compute revenue, so any China upside would be extra. Meanwhile, Nvidia has beaten the consensus guidance in 7 of the last 8 quarters, which makes a beat the base case. Last quarter, revenue came in at $96.2 B, which represented +106% year over year. Also, Data Center revenue reached $89 B, +117%. However, gross margin guidance of 74% is below the 75% reported last quarter. The average analyst price target sits at $277. Citi kept a $225 price target with a Buy rating. On the technical side, $158 level is the initial support for now and the next support level sits at $135. On the upside, $174 is the initial resistance level. Any close above $166 could keep a move toward the initial resistance level. However, any close below $158 could drag the prices towards $135. Meanwhile, investors will be watching tomorrow’s earnings release, the guidance for next quarter, and any update on a permanent CEO.

Nvidia (NVDA) stock fell 4% on Monday as investors weighed tighter US restrictions on overseas access to advanced AI semiconductors and a report that supporters of Jensen Huang are lobbying for his return to the chip heavyweight following his abrupt resignation last week. Huang has discussed returning as CEO with confidants, the Financial Times reported Sunday, citing people familiar with the matter. Huang resigned last week following reports of affairs, including one with a woman who was reportedly suspected of being a Chinese spy. This price reflects trading activity during the overnight session on the Blue Ocean ATS, available 8 PM to 4 AM ET, Sunday through Thursday, when regular markets are closed. According to the report, a Huang supporter said that a "war room" of Silicon Valley executives was being assembled to lobby Nvidia's board to reinstate him, including by seeking support from the White House. "Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen," the person said, adding that Huang supported the effort. On Monday, CNBC reported that the board was not considering bringing Huang back to the company. Meanwhile, SpaceX (SPCX) and Tesla (TSLA) CEO Elon Musk has come out in support of Huang, writing on X last Friday, "A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen, and I'm signing it too." On Saturday, Musk said, "Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia, but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract. Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost." The push to bring Huang back comes days after the FT reported that Nvidia's board had approached Arm Holdings (ARM) CEO Rene Haas as it searches for a successor. Nvidia CFO Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO during the search. Yorkville's Dan Ives said that while no "one individual can replace Jensen as CEO," any talk of "Jensen coming back to Nvidia is ridiculous in our view given the legal/Board/DC scrutiny/moral compass/China tentacles." This price reflects trading activity during the overnight session on the Blue Ocean ATS, available 8 PM to 4 AM ET, Sunday through Thursday, when regular markets are closed. Huang abruptly stepped down Thursday following reports of alleged affairs with a former executive from Singapore-based Megaspeed, and also an Nvidia employee who reported directly to him. Days earlier, Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife but did not disclose how many affairs he had or identify those involved. Recent reports have raised concerns about whether restricted semiconductors were being diverted to China and if sensitive US information had been sent to Beijing. The developments have also sent shockwaves through the AI industry, where Nvidia has played a central role in building the ecosystem. The company has become a bellwether for the AI trade and has invested in key parts of the industry, including large language model development, energy, optics, and cloud providers. Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly results Tuesday after the bell in what will be the company's first earnings call without Huang. Nvidia stock declined more than 12% last week, closing below a $4 trillion market cap. At least 10 Wall Street analysts have recently downgraded the stock from Buy to Hold, with many citing, in part, increased scrutiny in Washington and succession uncertainty. title: The tech world's calls for Jensen Huang to return to Nvidia are growing - CNBC
content:
An online petition calling for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO has drawn nearly 180,000 signatures, as prominent tech executives, employees and shareholders rally behind him following his resignation last week. The “Stand with Jensen” campaign has attracted support from Elon Musk, Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney. It comes as the Financial Times reported that Huang has discussed the possibility of returning as Nvidia’s chief executive with close confidants, citing multiple people familiar with the matter. “A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen and I’m signing it too,” Musk posted Friday on X. Tan also posted he’d signed, saying: “Jensen deserves due process, not whatever is happening right now.” Sweeney posted “save Jensen!” on Sunday as he shared the petition. Other high-profile signatories include Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke and former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick, who both confirmed their signatures on X. Hugging Face CEO Julien Chaumond is also listed as having signed. CNBC found dozens of signatories identifying themselves as current and former Nvidia employees, though the website notes that affiliations are self-reported and not verified. Huang, who co-founded the company in 1993 and helped turn it into a dominant supplier of artificial intelligence chips, resigned as Nvidia’s president, CEO and board member following reports of extramarital affairs — including one involving a woman suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence. The growing campaign for his reinstatement comes as the board seeks internal and external candidates to succeed him, and longtime finance chief Colette Kress serves as interim CEO. Any potential return, however, faces significant hurdles. Nvidia’s board is continuing an independent investigation into the conduct that led to Huang’s departure. U.S. lawmakers are preparing to investigate how Huang’s affair may have damaged America’s artificial intelligence dominance, the national security implications and his close relationship with President Donald Trump and his Cabinet. Speaking to reporters before departing for a series of summits in Asia Monday, Trump said he “would not mind” if Huang returned, adding that he thought the former CEO had learned a “big lesson.” The petition calls on Nvidia’s board to ensure a fair investigation into Huang’s conduct and provide greater transparency around the circumstances of his departure. Some Nvidia employees have also publicly expressed support for Huang, with one engineer saying he had decided to leave the company following the CEO’s departure. Darrell Dai, who identified himself as a robotics engineer at Nvidia, said Huang’s vision and the engineering culture he fostered were key reasons he had stayed at the company. Vartika Singh, who said she had worked at the chipmaker for nearly eight years, praised Huang’s leadership and personal support during a family medical crisis. “I have never worked for anyone quite like Jensen Huang, and I doubt I ever will,” Singh wrote on X, describing his commitment to employees, researchers and startups. The push has also gained traction among major shareholders, with Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker urging Nvidia’s board to consider all options, including Huang’s potential return, in an open letter Friday. The investors called for a measured approach to choosing Nvidia’s next leader, arguing that Huang deserved a fair process before the board made any permanent decision. Neil Shah, vice president of research at Counterpoint Research, told CNBC’s “Squawk Box Europe” on Monday that a potential Huang comeback would be “good for the stock.” “Jensen’s rhythm has made this AI ecosystem what it is right now,” Shah told CNBC’s Karen Tso and Steve Sedgwick. “The trillion-dollar capex, which has been spent every year, has to continue to make this train [keep] going.” Shah said his only concern is whether Nvidia would impose new guardrails on Huang, preventing him from leading the business with the same level of energy and enthusiasm. “If he cannot work freely and actually take the ecosystem on the same breadth and speed, will he be that effective? That is the big question.” One of Huang’s allies told the FT that supporters were assembling a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his reinstatement and would seek backing from the White House. The efforts had Huang’s support, the person added, according to the report. “We are in the process of selecting a search firm for the NVIDIA CEO role. We have not formally engaged any potential candidates,” an Nvidia spokesperson said in response to CNBC’s request for comment on the company’s search. The spokesperson added that any speculation about individual candidates, whether internal or external, was premature. Anthony Scaramucci, founder of alternative investment firm SkyBridge and a former White House communications director, also dismissed the prospect of Huang returning as CEO, saying the investigations surrounding him presented obstacles that a public campaign could not overcome. “The tech bros want Jensen back. Not happening,” Scaramucci wrote on X, arguing that Nvidia’s board could not reinstate a chief executive whose conduct remained under investigation. In a separate post, Scaramucci rejected comparisons with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who returned to the company days after being ousted in 2023. “The FBI doesn’t take petitions,” he wrote, saying that Huang’s situation was fundamentally different from Altman’s. Altman’s ouster stemmed from an internal governance dispute, while Huang’s situation involves ongoing investigations into his conduct that make a swift board reversal far more difficult. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday that Nvidia needs to look outside the company for its next executive. “I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?” he said in an interview with Fox News. Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company linked to the controversy, said recent media reports contained assertions about its business and supply chain that were not supported by verifiable evidence. The company said it had retained external legal counsel to conduct an internal investigation and that Alice Huang, a woman reportedly romantically linked to Jensen Huang and an alleged Chinese spy, left Megaspeed effective Aug. 30, 2025, and no longer holds any role there. Alice Huang may have owned stakes in businesses in China that benefited Nvidia’s biggest competitor in China, Huawei, CNBC reported earlier. Meanwhile, Nvidia’s board has approached Arm CEO Rene Haas as a potential successor to Huang, the FT reported. Nvidia’s board said at the time that it had not formally engaged any candidates. Some analysts see a path for Huang to return despite the controversy surrounding his departure. Jay Goldberg, a senior analyst at Seaport Research Partners, said Huang could make a comeback if he overcomes his legal challenges, citing his influence in the AI industry and continued support from investors. “If he can get through the legal trouble, I think we’ll have a second act from him,” Goldberg told CNBC’s “Squawk Box Asia.” But not everyone on Wall Street is convinced it can happen so soon. “We see no chance Jensen comes back to Nvidia as CEO,” Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., said in a note. Ives said the shareholder petition and public pressure could create further distractions for Nvidia, but would not change the central task facing interim CEO Kress: restoring stability and investor confidence. Ives added that Nvidia’s leadership in AI chips and its long-term demand outlook remained intact despite the management upheaval. Nvidia is scheduled to report its fiscal third-quarter earnings Tuesday, putting Kress and the company’s leadership team under the spotlight as investors look for reassurance about its future. — CNBC’s Caleigh Keating contributed to this report. "No further investment without Jensen," billionaire Leo KoGuan told Bloomberg (1) in a text message, a day after Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO. KoGuan, best known as one of the largest individual shareholders in Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) and worth about $13.2 billion by Bloomberg's estimate, said he has put about $1.3 billion into the chipmaker, though Bloomberg couldn't independently verify that figure. His pledge covers new purchases; he didn't say he'd sell the shares he already owns. Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993, resigned as president, CEO and board member effective immediately, Nvidia announced Nov. 12. The board accepted his resignation Nov. 11, according to a regulatory filing. CFO Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO, and the board said Nov. 13 it was still choosing a search firm to find a permanent replacement. Huang himself has been involved in that search and has personally contacted at least one potential candidate, The Washington Post reported (2), citing people familiar with the matter. Two heavyweight fund managers, whose names also appear on the petition, have asked the board to pump the brakes in a formal letter. Here's why the money crowd is so rattled — and why the risk for shareholders may not end with who runs the company. KoGuan hasn't been subtle. On X (5), he called Huang "the supreme creator" and said he hopes to invest in any new company Huang starts or buys. That's a change of pace for an investor who was loading up earlier this year. In March, KoGuan said he'd doubled his Nvidia stake (6) to 2 million shares. Two of Wall Street's best-known tech investors are taking a more measured line. On Nov. 13, Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management's Gavin Baker sent a joint letter (7) to Nvidia's board. Their ask was narrower than the petition's: "a slow, measured, and deliberate process regarding the future leadership of Nvidia that leaves all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang." "There are more questions about recent events than answers," they wrote, adding that the board "should avoid a rush to replace Jensen that undermines and thwarts the best interests of shareholders." They also conceded the final call isn't theirs. If the board decides Huang's return isn't in shareholders' best interest, "that is the Board's prerogative," the letter says. The support started before Huang resigned. On Nov. 8, Pershing Square CEO Bill Ackman wrote on X (8) that Huang "is an incredible human" and that "we should all support him and his family." He added that he wasn't suggesting Huang get "a free pass." Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao called it a mistake (9) for Nvidia to let Huang go. Shareholders have had a rough few weeks. Musk isn't a neutral observer, though. His rocket and AI company, SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX), is a major Nvidia customer, and Nvidia owns a stake in SpaceX worth billions. Not everyone is heading for the exits. Retail investors poured about $1.6 billion (14) into Nvidia shares over three days this week, Business Today reported, citing market data.
